title: Totem Poles, Kitseukla

image.credit: Vancouver Art Gallery, Canada; via arthistoryproject.com

altText: Tall carved poles stand upright in an outdoor setting, painted with strong colors and simplified, rounded shapes. Trees and sky surround them, and the brushwork is loose and energetic.

source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, year, medium, collection, public-domain statement)

context: An oil painting on canvas by Emily Carr, made in 1912 and now in the Vancouver Art Gallery in Canada. Kitseukla is a place in British Columbia, and the page tags the painting with totem poles.

descriptions.k: Tall carved poles stand in a row. They reach up toward the sky. The colors are bold. Look at how tall they are. What shapes or faces can you find? What story might they tell?
descriptions.g12: Emily Carr painted tall totem poles in a place called Kitseukla in Canada. The poles stand up high, and the paint is bold and loose. The poles carry carved shapes and designs. What shapes do you see on them? Why do you think they are so tall?
descriptions.g35: Emily Carr painted Totem Poles, Kitseukla in 1912 with oil on canvas. Kitseukla is a place in British Columbia, Canada, and the poles are carved cultural works made by Indigenous peoples of the Northwest Coast. Carr used strong colors and loose brushwork. How do the tall shapes and bold color make the poles feel powerful?
descriptions.g68: Carr's Totem Poles, Kitseukla (1912) shows carved poles in British Columbia in bold color and simplified form influenced by modern French painting. Totem poles are cultural works of Indigenous peoples of the Northwest Coast, so teachers may wish to consult the relevant community. How does Carr's style shape what you see, and what do you want to learn from the people connected to the poles?
descriptions.g910: Emily Carr's Totem Poles, Kitseukla (1912) combines Post-Impressionist color and simplified form with a subject drawn from Indigenous cultures of the Northwest Coast. Vertical poles dominate the composition and give it monumental presence. Because the poles hold cultural meanings, community context matters. How do the formal choices shape your response, and what limits does an outside painter's view carry? Look closely at the poles and their setting.
descriptions.g1112: Carr's Totem Poles, Kitseukla (1912) shows how she adapted modern European painting to a Northwest Coast subject. The monumental verticals and simplified forms give the poles presence, yet the painting is an outsider's view of cultural works whose meanings belong to the communities connected to them. Carr's work has been both celebrated and critiqued. How do we weigh artistic achievement and representation, and whose voices should guide the reading? Weigh the evidence in the poles, the color and the setting.

teacherNote.context: An oil painting made in 1912 by Emily Carr, now in the Vancouver Art Gallery. It shows totem poles at Kitseukla, a place in British Columbia; the poles are cultural works of Indigenous peoples, and teachers may wish to consult the relevant community for guidance on teaching this work.
directions: Invite students to design a tall banner that tells a story about their own family or community using simple shapes, and share what the symbols mean to them.
Have students look for materials made by the relevant Indigenous community or by Indigenous museums to learn how the community describes these poles.
Discuss what it means to depict something that belongs to another culture respectfully, and what an artist might do first.
